title: Physisorption vs. Chemisorption

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — Surface Chemistry

summary: Adsorption is the accumulation of a substance at a surface. Physisorption involves weak van der Waals forces; chemisorption involves the formation of actual chemical bonds between the adsorbate and the surface.
explanation: Physisorption is a weak, reversible process driven by van der Waals forces, occurs readily at low temperature, has a low enthalpy of adsorption, and can form multiple molecular layers. Chemisorption involves genuine chemical bond formation between adsorbate and adsorbent, is generally irreversible, has a much higher enthalpy of adsorption, is typically limited to a single molecular layer (monolayer), and often requires activation energy (so it may increase with temperature up to a point, unlike physisorption). Both processes are surface phenomena, distinct from absorption, where a substance is taken up into the BULK of a material rather than staying at the surface.

comparison.left: Physisorption: weak van der Waals forces

commonMisconceptions: Using 'adsorption' and 'absorption' interchangeably — adsorption is a SURFACE phenomenon, absorption involves uptake into the BULK of the material.
examples: Physisorption: gas molecules weakly held on activated charcoal at low temperature. Chemisorption: hydrogen chemically bonding to a nickel catalyst surface during hydrogenation.
genZNote: Physisorption is a loose hangout (weak attraction, easy to leave). Chemisorption is a committed relationship (actual bonds formed, much harder to walk away from).
